# LaunchSense

LaunchSense checks the codebase, not the business. One lane, local. The check runs on your machine, reads your working tree, sends nothing to us, and has no hourly limit.

This repository is the public half: the check engine and the skill. The website, the policies, and the backend live in a separate private repository, `launchsense-core`. The policy text still reaches your tool through the policy source.

This stage is alpha. Alpha has no login.

## Setup

Local reads the files. Online serves the policies. Your tool reads the rules from the policy source, guided by the skill, and the model writes the audit locally.

Local server, stdio, installed by `./install.sh` with `LAUNCHSENSE_ROOT` at your checkout:

```
node <checkout>/mcp/server.ts
```

Policy source, online, static coaching material only, never a scan:

```
https://harmless-chihuahua-667.convex.site/mcp
```

Cursor holds both entries as `launchsense` and `launchsense-policy`. Claude Code:

```
claude mcp add launchsense-policy --transport http https://harmless-chihuahua-667.convex.site/mcp
```

The online client POSTs one JSON-RPC message and gets one JSON answer. A call is counted, with no gate.

## Installing from a coding agent

`public/install.txt` is a plain-text brief for a coding agent. It asks the person the two permission questions first, then clones this repo, runs `./install.sh`, registers both servers for whichever harness it is, fetches the policy bundle once, and runs the first audit. One approval covers the whole first run.

## Tools

Online policy source, one closed and argument-free tool: `launchsense_get_policy`, which returns the whole bundle in one call. No repo URL, no file reads, no scans, no stored code. The skill fetches it once and keeps a local copy, so later runs make no policy calls and ask for no approvals.

Local review runs `launchsense_scan_repo` against `LAUNCHSENSE_ROOT`. It takes one optional argument, `mode`: `tree` (the default) reviews the whole working tree, and `change` reviews only what changed since the base of the branch, named in the report. OSV covers up to 50 packages. `launchsense_report` reads the latest local report under `.ls/reports`. `launchsense_github` reports the local `gh` login. `launchsense_scan_public_notice` scans nothing: it names both doors so neither is mistaken for the other.

Every report states its own completeness, in the body and the JSON, where a harness reads it: the existing `status` field is extended to `complete` or `partial`, and `statusNote` carries one line, `Review complete.` or `Review incomplete: <reasons in words>`. Completeness is per applicable check, so a check that does not apply to this repo (an npm lockfile check on a Python repo) is not a reason, and a check that applies and did not run is. The direct CLI exits 2 on an incomplete run; an explicit `--lenient` prints a warning and exits 0 instead, except for a cap hit or a lockfile in hand that was never queried, which never return 0. Over MCP the same facts arrive as report text and `isError` is reserved for a review that could not run at all. On a `change` run, an acceptance newly added to `.ls/policy.yaml` since the last report is reported as one info row naming the rule and the path: a disclosure, never above info.

A partial result is not a pass.

A partial result is not a pass.

## Checks

Fixed checks cover secrets, code shapes, dependency names, license text, dependency license terms, and project hygiene, plus duplicate files and large files.

The local review reads the tree under caps: 5,000 files and 40MB in all, 100KB per file. It does not read vendored trees, installed packages or tool caches (`.venv`, `venv`, `site-packages`, `node_modules`, and the common Python and JS caches), `.progress`, or binary files. Anything past a cap is listed as not checked.

### The report

The report leads with the solution, not a wall of findings: START HERE, then the lead fix prompt and the next prompts to paste, each naming the file; then PLAN, the ordered fix steps, secrets first, each with its why, files, and checklist; then DETAIL, the findings, the not-checked list line for line, the licence suggestion, and one line pointing at the third-party notice file written beside the report.

### The licence declaration

For a project that commits an npm `package-lock.json` with a `packages` map, every installed package, direct and transitive, is read for the licence it declares. Where the lockfile has no `license` field and an installed `package.json` is available, that manifest is the fallback, and a lockfile that disagrees with it reads as Unknown. A declaration that is not an SPDX expression, such as `MIT/X11`, reads as Unknown. `UNLICENSED` reads as `LicenseRef-Proprietary-UNLICENSED`. An `OR` expression stays a choice. A bare `GPL-2.0` is kept as declared and marked deprecated. `GPL-2.0+` normalizes to `GPL-2.0-or-later`.

`shared/licensing/obligations.ts` holds one cited row per licence family: licence text, copyright notice, a NOTICE file where the licence has one, state of changes, source disclosure for copyleft, and the distribution clash for strong copyleft. It is a table of what a licence text asks for. It is not a legal engine, and it does not decide whether an obligation applies to how you ship.

`npm run notices` writes the third-party notice artifact from the committed lockfile. Same lockfile in, byte-identical file out. The local review carries the same text.

The guarded AI lookup runs only for an Unknown licence, only when a lane is supplied, and only with the package name, the version, and fixed wording in the prompt. The result is a suggestion with no rule id, no fingerprint, and no severity. No lane is wired in this release, so the path is refused and unknown stays unknown.

Not checked on any surface: yarn.lock, pnpm-lock.yaml, Cargo, Go and PyPI dependency licences, a vendored tree, a per-file SPDX header or REUSE.toml, and registry freshness. A lockfile with no `packages` map reads as incomplete, not as zero licences.

License lines are signals, not legal advice. Unknown stays unknown. A model may quote one next look. That quote is not a finding. The priority table always orders the report, and a decision model may reorder inside one severity band. The model does not choose which findings exist.

### What the AI does and does not decide

Three paths reach a model, and all three need a configured key, so the fixed paths are what run by default.

- `explain` rewrites a finding in plainer language. `shared/ai/deterministic.ts`.
- `ordering` reorders findings that already exist, inside one severity band. `shared/adapters/decision.ts`, `shared/reports/priority.ts`. The local review's report states the provenance in plain words, then the order source and the count of positions a model moved.
- `licence_lookup` suggests an id for an Unknown licence, refused unless a lane is supplied, never a licence fact. `shared/licensing/lookup.ts`.

The `humanOversightLevel` is `prompt_guided` in every case, which in C2PA Technical Specification 2.4 means a person provided the request and nobody approved the output. No path here is `fully_autonomous` and none is `human_validated`. The vocabulary is borrowed and this is not a conformance claim.

The AI never decides a finding, a severity, a licence fact, consent, who a caller is, or whether a request is allowed. `shared/copy/aiDisclosure.ts` is the single source of that list, with the file behind each item.

## Surfaces

Two addresses, two jobs. Local reads the files. Online serves the policies.

- The online policy source answers one closed tool with static text, `launchsense_get_policy`, returning the whole bundle in one call: version, skill, rules, checklist, and audit instructions. One call is one approval in the harness. No arguments, no repo URL, no file reads, no scans, no stored code. A call is counted with no gate.
- A local stdio MCP server (`mcp/server.ts`, wired by `install.sh`) reviews a checkout on that machine. It is a Node script and imports only Node builtins, so it starts with `node mcp/server.ts`. It needs Node 24 or newer on `PATH`; without Node the installer says so and registers no server.
- The governance file, `.ls/policy.yaml`, in the checkout the review reads. It is the repo's own memory: the findings a person already accepted, with a reason, so a later review does not raise them again. `shared/review/governance.ts` parses and validates it, and it is declarative only: no code, no anchors, no includes, no wildcards. A wrong file is refused whole and nothing is suppressed; a file that would silence more than half the findings by one acceptance, or four fifths in total, is refused whole. An accepted finding is removed from the findings list and named in the not-checked list as accepted, so a suppression is never silent. The folder is gitignored, and `mcp/review-entry.ts` writes one line to `.gitignore` the first time it creates it. `.ls/reports/<timestamp>.md` keeps a copy of each report next to the policy, written only when the local file read was acknowledged.
  - It speaks MCP over stdio as newline-delimited JSON: one JSON message per line in, one JSON message per line out, with no length header. `initialize` negotiates one of four protocol versions (2024-11-05, 2025-03-26, 2025-06-18, 2025-11-25) and answers 2025-03-26 when the client asks for nothing this server serves. Refused and error lines go to stderr, so stdout carries protocol only.
  - One message may be up to 4 MiB (4,194,304 bytes, the trailing newline included). A longer line is answered with a JSON-RPC error, nothing runs, and the next message is still answered.
  - Its tools are `launchsense_scan_repo`, which reviews the checkout and takes one optional `mode` argument (`tree`, the default, or `change`), `launchsense_report`, which reads the latest local report under `.ls/reports`, `launchsense_github`, which reports the local `gh` login, and `launchsense_scan_public_notice`, which scans nothing and names both doors so neither is mistaken for the other. A tool name this server does not have is a protocol error. An undeclared, wrong-typed, or wrong-enum argument is refused rather than ignored.
  - `launchsense_scan_repo` reviews `LAUNCHSENSE_ROOT`, which `install.sh` sets to the checkout root, so it reads the checkout and not the `mcp` folder. `LAUNCHSENSE_ROOT` must be absolute, and a folder that is not a checkout is named in the answer.
  - A report body over 1 MiB is refused and named, never returned as a whole report or a clipped success. The local review gives up after 10 minutes.
  - It reads files locally and does not upload them. Usage counts are off unless you answer yes to one question. `install.sh` asks before it records anything and defaults to no; it keeps the answer, with the wording it agreed to, in `~/.config/launchsense/consent.jsonl`. With a yes it sends rule id counts, the harness name, the version, how long it took, and which order source ran. That share carries no code, paths, titles, or function names. `install.sh --enterprise` and `LAUNCHSENSE_DIAGNOSTICS=off` leave it off.

## Standards records

Generated from facts in this repository, none claiming more than the code does.

- `npm run notices` writes the third-party notice file from the committed lockfile, deterministic: same lockfile in, byte-identical file out.
- `npm run sbom` writes a CycloneDX 1.7 SBOM from the same inventory the notice file reads, with SPDX ids and package URLs. Same lockfile in, byte-identical document out, so it carries no timestamp unless you pass `--generated-at`. No hashes, because no tarball was downloaded, and no dependency graph, because the inventory carries no edges. An Unknown licence is written as the name `Unknown` with its reason, never as an id.
- The licence suggestion, in `shared/licensing/suggest.ts`. It reads the licence ids and counts the repo declares, plus the repo allowlist from `.ls/policy.yaml`, and suggests one pick with a reason. It is a suggestion, never a licence fact, and it never writes a finding or a severity. Copyleft, source-available, and proprietary terms decline. The lane state carries licence ids and counts only: no package name, no path, no file text.
- The standards mapping, in `shared/reports/standards.ts`. Each row labels findings the checks already made onto OWASP Top 10:2025, OWASP ASVS 5.0.0, CWE, CWE Top 25 (2024), NIST SSDF 1.1, SLSA 1.0, OSV, deps.dev, or OpenSSF Scorecard. A row is `partial` only where a check exists; everything else stays `not-checked`. `standardsCoverage()` reports two numbers that are never merged: what the product can check at all, and what this scan actually found. It is a signal, never a certification. Licensed frameworks (ISO, SOC 2, PCI, SIG, CAIQ) are cited by name only, never embedded.

## Analytics

A call to the policy source is counted on the server, because the call is to our service. No gate is placed on it, and the row carries the method and the outcome only, never a repository URL, file text, or a network address. Local audits are counted only if the person opts in. No PII either way.

## Do not claim

The review does not say the app will sell. It does not edit the repo. It does not certify anything. It does not treat a source-available license as open source.
